# Rudd dumping cost votes: survey

Mark Davis

April 8, 2011 — 12:00am

AN OVERWHELMING majority of voters who swung away from Labor at last year's federal election were unhappy with the way Kevin Rudd was dumped as Prime Minister, according to a new survey.

The Australian Election Study - a detailed ''exit survey'' of voters from last year's election - found that one in four people who had voted Labor in 2007 changed their first preference to another party at the 2010 poll.

The survey found that 79 per cent of these voters switching support away from Labor disapproved of the way the ALP handled its leadership change when Julia Gillard replaced Mr Rudd last June. By comparison, 64 per cent of the people who voted Labor in 2007 and then stuck with the ALP at the 2010 election said they disapproved of the way Mr Rudd was ousted.

The survey results provide the first hard evidence of the impact of Labor's leadership change on its electoral support at last year's poll.

The study by a team of researchers from the Australian National University and Queensland University of Technology surveyed 2214 voters on how they voted and their attitudes to a range of election issues and political leaders.

Despite widespread disapproval of the way Labor handled its leadership change, the survey found that Ms Gillard and Mr Rudd had similar levels of ''likeability'' among voters and that both were significantly more popular than the Liberal leader, Tony Abbott. Forty six per cent of voters said they liked Ms Gillard, 38 per cent disliked her . Mr Rudd had virtually identical figures (44 per cent liked him, 39 per cent didn't). By contrast just 37 per cent of voters said they liked Mr Abbott and 47 per cent said they didn't.
